assignments.description:
A report back on another site that is facing similar issues of inequitable or harmful development and/or gentrification either on or around campus or elsewhere in New Jersey. The purpose is for you to connect some of the concepts we’ve discussed to your daily environment. (Most ideally, examples you have not brought up already in our group discussions). Your presentation should be able to explain the background and significance of your chosen site to all of us who may be unaware of the context. You are also encouraged to discuss what the opposing views are (eg. those who are in favor of the development). Please bring visuals.

You must also submit here a 750 word write up afterwards that presents your own viewpoint of the development, whether that be for, against, or mixed. This write up should not just be stating opinions but should be backing up your viewpoint through citing theoretical or cultural texts we’ve discussed.

assignments.description:
Option 1: You may revise your midterm essay by expanding it and adding an additional cultural text for a more comparative analysis of the concept and texts. For example, if you chose Lowe's Intimacies of Four Continents and Pete Pin's "Migrations of Memory" in your midterm, you could then bring in a second cultural text such as Tseng Kwon Chi's photography to discuss the aesthetic, formal and rhetorical strategies of how both artists address the concept of intimacy. The midterm page limit was about 5 pages double spaced, handwritten. The revision should be about 10-12 pages typed, double spaced (approximately 6000 words).

Option 2: You may choose to write an entirely new essay from this prompt: What concept or argument from our course changed your prior thinking about the relationship between power, race and space/placemaking? Or, if you didn't experience any major revelations, what existing belief about power, race, and space/placemaking did you have confirmed and why/how? You must discuss at length one of the theoretical texts we have read and one cultural text from the course or from outside (that you provide a link or access to so that I may view it). This essay should be thesis and argument driven. 

Crucially, for a full grade, you must also reference a discussion we had in class on the same text/topic. This may include: something that a colleague said in one of our discussions that sparked something in your thinking (or that you disagreed with); an example or visual that the instructor brought up; or something that felt unsatisfactory or unexplained in the texts and our discussion of it. Most ideally, you would include more than one of the above as you reference our class discussions. The essay should be 10-12 pages, double spaced.

Based on the Princeton exam schedule, the due date is Thursday, December 18th at 3:30pm

Chemistry 201, General Chemistry I, is Princeton’s introductory course to the study of chemistry.

It is the first of a two-part series. In this course we will cover the basic concepts of atomic structure, stoichiometry, reactions, gases, equilibrium, thermodynamics, and bonding. This course is designed to not only introduce the concepts that form the foundations of modern chemistry, but also to demonstrate how these concepts explain the molecular interactions that make up our world!

Please reference our syllabus below for details on scheduling, assignments, contact information, and course policies.

The McGraw Center for Teaching and Learning, located in the Frist Campus Center, is an excellent resource for your academic journeys here at Princeton! For CHM 201 specifically, they offer the following:

Course Specific Peer Tutoring

The McGraw Center's main mode of peer tutoring is drop-in group study hall, a three-hour period where students can stay for as long or as little as they like and work with both the peer tutors present and their classmates. They expect to offer study hall twice each week (dependent on staffing) starting on Monday 9/8. Their regular tutoring schedule will not be set until the second or third week of the semester.

Depending on staffing they plan to offer individual peer tutoring as well, which would start Sunday 9/15. Individual tutoring will have limited availability, so they encourage students to visit study hall as well.

Academic Life & Learning Strategies Consultations

The McGraw Center also offers other forms of learning support, including Academic Life & Learning Strategies Consultations. These are hour-long meetings between a student and a learning consultant (third and fourth year Princeton students). Students can use these appointments for any questions or problems related to academics. Students can book appointments at schedule.princeton.edu (there are already appointments available) and more information can be found on their website.

Academic Strategies Workshops

In addition to tutoring and learning consultations the McGraw Center also offers Academic Strategies Workshops on a different topic each week. These are hands-on, active, and process-focused workshops in which students learn and apply strategies designed expressly for the highly demanding Princeton University context. A few of the upcoming workshops include:

  • Strategies for Success – 9/9 & 9/15
  • Time Management for Balance & Success – 9/11 & 9/13
  • Approach Academics Like Athletic, Artistic & Other Performances – 9/16
  • Efficient Reading Strategies for Reading-Intensive Courses – 9/18
  • Efficient Reading Strategies for STEM+ Courses – 9/20
  • Strategies for Tacking STEM P-Sets and Preparing for Exams – 9/23

See the McGraw Center's website for more information.
